title: Storage Engines: B-Trees vs LSM-Trees
subtitle: Write-Ahead Logs, MemTables, SSTable compaction vs in-place B-Tree page splits
overview: Why do Cassandra and RocksDB ingest hundreds of thousands of writes per second while PostgreSQL shines on predictable point reads and complex indexes? The answer lies inside the storage engine on disk: append-only Log-Structured Merge-Trees (LSM-Trees) versus page-oriented B-Trees.
firstPrinciplesStory: Imagine you are building an append-only audit log for 100,000 events/sec. You start with a single flat file—writes are blazingly fast sequential appends, until you realize searching for one key requires scanning gigabytes. Adding a sorted B-Tree solves lookups in O(log N) page hops, yet random writes now bounce disk heads/NVMe pages across 4 KB blocks, triggering write amplification and dirty-page splits. What if you keep writes purely sequential in RAM + WAL and merge sorted immutable segments asynchronously in the background? That tension—sequential writes vs predictable read latency—is the core story of DDIA Chapter 3.

adaptiveLenses.intuition: A B-Tree is like an alphabetically sorted filing cabinet: finding a folder is instant, but squeezing a new folder into a full drawer forces shifting folders and splitting drawers on the spot. An LSM-Tree is like dropping notes onto your desk pad in arrival order, then sorting stacks neatly into labeled boxes at night—instant drop-off, occasional cleanup tax, and searching might check 2–3 boxes unless you keep a sticky-note checklist (Bloom filter).
adaptiveLenses.mechanics: LSM engines append mutations to a disk WAL for durability and insert sorted keys into an in-memory Red-Black/SkipList MemTable. When full, the MemTable flushes sequentially as an immutable SSTable (Sorted String Table) with sparse index + per-SSTable Bloom filter. Background Leveled/Size-Tiered Compaction merges overlapping SSTables and drops tombstones. B-Trees mutate fixed 4–16 KB pages in place (buffered via Page Cache + WAL recovery), using latch crabbing for concurrent tree traversal.
adaptiveLenses.staffTradeoffs: Evaluate write, read and space amplification together (the RUM Conjecture). LSM trees win on write throughput by turning random writes into sequential ones, and they compress tightly, which suits write-heavy time-series and messaging (RocksDB, Cassandra, ScyllaDB). They do not have lower write amplification everywhere: leveled compaction commonly rewrites each byte 10 to 30 times in exchange for low space and read amplification, while size-tiered compaction writes less but uses more space and makes reads check more files. Unbounded compaction also steals disk IOPS and causes p99 spikes, whereas B-Trees offer tight p99 read bounds and clean range and lock semantics for OLTP.

ddiaAnchors.whyItMatters: Explains why write-heavy workloads pick LSM engines while OLTP transactional stores rely on B-Tree indexes.
Explains why LSM p99 read latency can spike unpredictably during heavy SSTable merges.

pragmaticTips.tip: Never pick NoSQL/LSM or SQL/B-Tree on hype—benchmark your read:write ratio, key distribution, and p99 sensitivity first.
pragmaticTips.application: If writes are <5k QPS and relational ACID matters, boring B-Tree Postgres beats operational complexity every time.

pragmaticTips.tip: Uncapped LSM compaction can starve foreground user queries of NVMe bandwidth.
pragmaticTips.application: Rate-limit compaction throughput and monitor L0 SSTable stall thresholds proactively.

keyTakeaways: LSM-Trees convert random application writes into fast sequential RAM + WAL appends and periodic SSTable flushes.
Per-SSTable Bloom filters prevent LSM point reads for non-existent keys from probing every L0–L3 SSTable on disk.
B-Trees store one authoritative copy of each key in fixed-size pages, avoiding multi-level read checks and compaction pauses.

nodes.label: Storage Write Client
nodes.summary: Issues high-rate random key mutations and point lookups.
whenToUse: Write-heavy telemetry, messaging, or KV stores
failureModes: Random UUID keys destroy B-Tree cache locality under write load

nodes.label: Write-Ahead Log (WAL)
nodes.summary: Append-only crash recovery log guaranteeing durability before acking MemTable writes.
whenToUse: Both B-Trees and LSM-Trees depend on WAL for crash safety
failureModes: Unbounded WAL growth if MemTable flushes stall

nodes.label: In-Memory MemTable
nodes.summary: Maintains recent writes sorted in RAM and flips immutable once size threshold is hit.
whenToUse: Absorbing burst writes at memory speed
failureModes: OOM or write stalls if flush thread falls behind

nodes.label: Immutable SSTables (L0–L2)
nodes.summary: Sorted immutable disk segments paired with in-RAM Bloom filters and sparse key offsets.
failureModes: Too many overlapping L0 files degrade read latency rapidly

nodes.label: B-Tree Engine (Comparison)
nodes.summary: Updates fixed pages in place; single authoritative key location makes reads & row locks clean.
whenToUse: OLTP transactional SQL, predictable point/range queries
failureModes: Random key inserts dirty entire buffer pool causing write amplification

steps.info: PUT user:4812 appended sequentially to the WAL buffer (0 random disk seeks)
steps.inspectorNote: Even in an LSM-Tree, every accepted write hits the append-only WAL first so a crash doesn't wipe the volatile MemTable.

steps.info: WAL batch fsync'd to stable storage (group commit every ~1–2 ms) before any ack
steps.payloadInspector: fdatasync(wal-000184.log) covers 512 writes in one flush -> durable at LSN 994102
steps.inspectorNote: Durability depends on the fsync policy, not on the append. Cassandra's default commitlog_sync=periodic (10 s) and RocksDB's default WriteOptions.sync=false can both lose acknowledged writes on power loss; group commit makes per-write sync affordable.

steps.info: Key inserted in O(log N) into RAM SkipList -> write ACK returned after the WAL fsync
steps.payloadInspector: MemTable usage: 63.9 MB / 64.0 MB -> write acknowledged at 1.35 ms (fsync included)
steps.inspectorNote: Notice how fast random writes complete—zero B-Tree page splitting or random 4 KB page dirties on disk.

steps.info: MemTable freezes -> flushed sequentially as L0 SSTable + Bloom filter; WAL truncated
steps.inspectorNote: Because keys are already sorted in the MemTable, flushing to disk is one blazing sequential write.

predictPrompt.prompt: If a read requests a key `user:9999999` that does NOT exist in the database, what happens inside an LSM-Tree without a Bloom Filter?
predictPrompt.hint: Think about how many immutable L0..L3 SSTables might contain overlapping key ranges.
predictPrompt.reveal: Without per-SSTable Bloom filters, a lookup for a missing key must check MemTable AND probe every L0 file plus every deeper level (L1, L2, L3...) on disk—multiplying read latency by 5x–10x!

steps.info: Contrast: random key on B-Tree forces 4 KB page read-modify-write & split
steps.payloadInspector: B-Tree Page #4012 full -> allocate Page #4013 -> rewrite 2 leaf pages + parent pointer
steps.inspectorNote: B-Trees trade higher random-write amplification for single-place key lookup and predictable OLTP range/lock performance.

chaosScenarios.title: L0 SSTable Pileup & Compaction Tail-Latency Spike
chaosScenarios.triggerSummary: Burst writes outpace background compaction, piling up 24 overlapping L0 SSTables and saturating NVMe disk I/O.
chaosScenarios.mitigationSummary: Engine triggers intentional write backpressure (L0 stall) while prioritizing L0→L1 leveled compaction and isolating compaction IOPS.

steps.info: L0 count=24 -> reads probe 24 overlapping files; compaction saturates NVMe queue
steps.payloadInspector: Read p99 jumps 1ms -> 48ms | Compaction I/O consuming 85% disk bandwidth
steps.inspectorNote: DDIA Ch. 3 warns that background compaction steals disk bandwidth from user reads—causing silent p99 spikes.

steps.info: Engine throttles foreground ingest briefly + caps compaction MB/s -> L0 drops to 4
steps.payloadInspector: Rate-limited compaction preserves 40% NVMe headroom for foreground reads -> p99 recovers
steps.inspectorNote: Bounding background work and applying early backpressure prevents cascading storage stalls.

pros: Tighter compression (no half-empty B-Tree page fragmentation)
cons: Reads check MemTable + multiple SSTable levels (Bloom filters required)
Background compaction causes p99 I/O jitter
tradeoffs.bestFor: Write-heavy messaging, time-series metrics, event logs, embedded KV engines

pros: Each key lives in exactly one page—predictable point/range reads
Clean page/row locking for ACID transactions
cons: Higher random write amplification on non-sequential keys (UUIDv4)
tradeoffs.bestFor: Relational OLTP workloads with complex queries, transactions, and mixed read/write
